blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Evaluating Memory Policies**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Long-Term Memory, § Evaluating Memory Policies
blocks.md: Excluding a stale failure trace from an earlier run keeps an outdated representation out of the agent's next request, but it does not ensure that the agent finds the fresh evidence needed to effect a repair. Conversely, a stored reflection might reproduce a recent passing test run accurately while overstating what the pass proves. Rigorous evaluation cannot treat memory as a static lookup table.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Cross-session policy trials
- Retrieval relevance judgments
- Lifecycle outcomes and full costs
- Adversarial boundary tests

questions.q: The section **Evaluating Memory Policies** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Persistent records are roles in an evidence chain (source of record, observation log, agent-written memory, retrieval index), not storage tiers, and any claim is validated against its source of record.
A retrieval index is a materialized view that cannot be maintained by deltas, so each derived entry carries a source generation and the gateway admits it only for the generations it is valid in.

The unit of evaluation is the whole memory policy run through isolated multi-session trials with lifecycle fixtures, scored by task acceptance and cost per accepted task including background maintenance.

Repeated retrieval or re-summarization adds no independent evidence, so preventing a withdrawn or unverified claim from persisting needs a provenance graph over derived records whose invalidation cascades.
